La idea de apartar datos para evaluar es: The idea of setting data aside to evaluate is surprisingly modern. Cross-validation, which consists of rotating which piece is set aside so as to use all the data, was formalised by Mervyn Stone and Seymour Geisser in two papers of 1974 and 1975. Before that the usual thing was to judge a model by how well it fitted the data that had produced it, which is exactly what this topic advises against. The theory that explains why a model that gets a sample right should get things right outside it is Vapnik and Chervonenkis's, the same one behind [[ia-margen|support vector machines]].

It reads: “L total is L of the data plus lambda times the sum of the weights squared”.

The $\lambda$ sets the price. With $\lambda = 0$ there is no penalty and the model does as it pleases; with an enormous $\lambda$, the only way of not paying is to set every weight to zero, and the model becomes a flat line. In between is the interesting part, and exactly where is decided with the validation pile, not by eye.

It reads: “n plus one points imply a polynomial of degree n with zero error”.

It is a theorem, not a coincidence: there are $n+1$ coefficients to determine and $n+1$ conditions to satisfy, and the system has a unique solution.

The consequence is uncomfortable: achieving zero error over the data you have proves absolutely nothing. It can always be done, by raising the degree enough. The good question is another: what the model does between the points, which is where it is really going to be used.

It is applied column by column: each with its own mean and its own deviation. Afterwards, they all have mean 0 and deviation 1, so none rules over the others just for coming in larger units.

And a detail that is always forgotten: $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are computed with the training data only. Using the validation ones to compute them is letting the model find out something it should not know.
